implementation_notes: JavaScript has no method overloading, so arguments contribute nothing to dispatch on their own; the language's replacement for the classic accept/visit round-trip is a lookup keyed by both dynamic types - typically a Map from a `${a.kind}:${b.kind}` (or constructor-keyed) string to a handler function. The matrix then lives in one readable place, costs one hash lookup per call, and works with classes, plain objects or discriminated tags. Keep the round-trip (see visitor-methods) for open type sets where third parties must add types without editing the table.
pitfalls: Keying on constructor.name breaks under minification or bundling: key on a stable `kind` field or on the constructor function itself.
A Map keyed by constructors holds strong references; handlers registered at runtime must be removable or the map grows for the process lifetime.
instanceof walks the prototype chain, so subclasses match their parent's cell: decide deliberately between exact-type and most-specific-type dispatch.

variants.name: Method round-trip (a.collideWith(b) -> b.collideWithCircle(a))
variants.idiom_name: receiver calls a method on the argument, passing itself
variants.implementation_notes: The canonical double dispatch survives in JavaScript because method lookup is dynamic: the receiver calls a method on the argument and passes itself, and the argument's method name encodes the receiver's type, because there is no overloading to do it implicitly. It stays open to new types - a new class ships its own methods - but each collaborator has to know every receiver type by name, exactly the scattering Beck and Fowler warn about. Use it when the element set is open and operations are few; otherwise a tag-keyed table is cheaper and easier to audit.
pitfalls: A pair with no method surfaces as a TypeError at call time - the language will not tell you a cell is missing.
Method names must be unique per receiver type, so the naming convention is the contract and typos surface only when that pair runs.
The round-trip costs two dynamic lookups per call; hoist handlers into a local table inside hot loops.
